howDoI.q: How do I make a pickup that adds one to a count?
How do I make a gate that wants all four?
How do I fill a room with a background pattern?
How do I make a block that changes when you bump it?
How do I make a door that opens when you bump it?
How do I make a gate that needs one thing first?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

Under the Hood is a Starter: a small game that shows a few ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has three short levels and takes a few minutes to finish.

This one is not about making a level. It is about the player: the DOS program (XFERPLAY.EXE in a DOS export) that runs every Game-Maker game. A program is a long row of bytes, and some of those bytes are the words its menu shows. Changing them is called patching.

None of these levels patches anything. They are ordinary levels that walk you through the ideas. The real thing is in chapter 17 of the Programmer’s Guide, Patching the player, and in the game editor’s DOS player panel, whose Patch Lab shows the bytes of each setting before and after you change it.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Space jumps. Up and Down climb a ladder. F2 shows your lives, hit points and score. Walk into the door at the end of a level to go on. Nothing in this game hurts you.

pages.head: Level 1: What Is an EXE
pages.html:
Level 1: What Is an EXE

The whole room is a hex dump: rows of bytes written as two hex digits each, the way a byte editor shows a file. The signs say what that means. AN EXE IS A LONG ROW OF BYTES, and EVERY BYTE HAS AN OFFSET: its place in the row, counted from 0.

The sign AT 2575B THE BYTES SAY PLAY stands before four bright bytes: 50, 6C, 61 and 79. Under each is its letter, P, l, a and y. That is where the DOS player really keeps the word on its menu: four bytes at offset 2575B (hex), with a zero byte after them to end the word.

Pick up all four. THE GATE WANTS ALL 4, and it opens when you carry them. Past it, the last sign says A PATCH LIVES IN THE PLAYER, NOT IN A LEVEL: a level is the game’s data, the menu words are the player’s. There are five coins on the way.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 1 is made

  • The hex dump. Open one.bbl in the blocks editor. The eight blocks after the panel are plain air, like the sky, each drawn with two rows of dim bytes in a tiny font. The map lays them on every open cell above the ground, in a repeating order, so the room reads like a page of a byte editor.
  • The green world. It is the Starter palette with the sky colors changed to a dark green and the grass and dirt to greens. The signs keep their cream paper, so they read on the dark screen.
  • A byte. Pick the 50 block. It is not solid. Its Changes counter is Special counter 3 by 1, and Becomes is the sky, so it is gone once you touch it. The other three are the same block idea with a different picture.
  • The gate. The Play gate is solid, its Changes counter is Special counter 3 by -4, and it Becomes the sky. A touch that the counter cannot pay is refused, so with three bytes it stays shut.
  • The real numbers. 50 6C 61 79 are the ASCII codes of P, l, a and y. Offset 2575B is from the table of the player’s settings that the editor’s DOS player panel uses.

pages.head: Level 2: Same Size
pages.html:
Level 2: Same Size

A WORD SITS IN A SLOT, and PLAY HAS 4 BYTES. SO DOES ITS SLOT. A new word has to fit the old word’s room.

A wall has two doors, each a four-byte slot drawn as a 2 by 2 grid of letters. The lower one tries START. START IS 5 BYTES. TOO LONG: S, T, A and R fill the slot and the last T sticks out. Walk into it and it jams red, NO ROOM. In a real player that fifth letter would land on the byte after the word and the next word, Read Instructions, would lose its first letter.

Climb the ladder to the upper door. GO AND 2 SPACES FITS: G, O, a space and a space are four bytes. Walk into it and it opens. Past the wall, SAME SIZE IN, SAME SIZE OUT. There are five coins on the way.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 2 is made

  • The START slot. Open two.bbl and pick the START plate. It is solid and its Becomes is the NO ROOM plate, which is solid too and becomes nothing. A bump swaps one picture for the other, and the way stays shut either way, which is the lesson: a word that is too long never fits.
  • The GO slot. The GO plate is solid and Becomes the sky, with no counter at all. A bump opens it.
  • Two doors. Each door is an arch block (air, drawn as the top of a doorway) over a plate, in a wall of solid panels that goes up to the top of the room, so neither can be jumped over. A ledge of panels and a ladder lead to the upper one.
  • Spaces. A space is shown as a short line, so you can count four bytes. The DOS player draws a space as nothing, which is why a shorter word padded with spaces looks right on its menu.

pages.head: Level 3: Ask First
pages.html:
Level 3: Ask First

The first sign says COPY THE EXE FIRST, and a blue disk labeled COPY lies just past it. THE GATE WANTS A BACKUP: pick up the disk and the gate opens.

Then the signs say the rest. ONLY CHANGE YOUR OWN COPY. A gold plaque saying CREDITS hangs over LEAVE THE CREDITS AS THEY ARE: the names of the people who made something stay as they are. UNLOCKING A PAID GAME IS NOT TAUGHT HERE: this game leaves that part alone. Last, TRY IT ON THE COPY, THEN PLAY. There are six coins on the way.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 3 is made

  • The disk. Open three.bbl and pick the disk. It is not solid; its Changes counter is Special counter 4 by 1, and it Becomes the sky.
  • The backup gate. It is solid, takes 1 from Special counter 4 and Becomes the sky. Without the disk the touch is refused. In the game the gate takes the count; with a real backup, keep the copy where it is.
  • The plaque. The CREDITS plaque is two air blocks hung on the hex dump. There is nothing to pick up or change, on purpose.
  • Each level’s own blocks. The three levels share the same ground, walls and pickups, but each level’s signs are its own blocks. All sixteen signs would not fit the 150 blocks one block file holds, so each scene loads its own block file: one.bbl, two.bbl and three.bbl.
  • The real steps. Patching the player walks through a patch one step at a time: copy the player, change one setting, keep the size, check every screen you changed.

pages.head: What Game-Maker cannot do
pages.html:
What Game-Maker cannot do

These levels show ideas about the player, and that is all they can do:

  • A level cannot change the player. A scene holds a map, blocks, a palette and text; the menu words, the status line, the timings and the F-keys are in the player program, so no level can show “the patched version” of them.
  • A block cannot check that a word fits. The START plate jams because it was drawn and set up to jam, not because anything counted its letters.
  • A counter is not shown on screen. The status line shows hit points, lives and score, not a special counter, so the gates show what they want in their pictures.
  • The player does not see the counter go back. The backup gate takes the disk’s count, as any gate does; there is no way to look at a counter without changing it.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

  • Change the Play gate’s amount to -3 in the blocks editor. It now opens with any three bytes.
  • Draw your own four-byte word on the bytes and the gate, say Quit (51 75 69 74).
  • Make the GO plate jam too, and give the upper door a different word that fits.
  • Change the palette back to the Starter sky and see how much of the look is the palette.
  • Then open your own game’s DOS player panel and change the Play word there. The Patch Lab shows the four bytes at 2575B change.

The home page’s Starters tab has more small games like this one.
